Every Saturday morning in their Hyderabad flat, Irawati closed her bedroom door at nine and did a full mock paper, three hours, timed on the kitchen clock.

On Saturday afternoon she didn't just look at the score. She took three coloured pens and went through every wrong answer. Red: didn't know the concept. Blue: knew it but made a silly mistake. Black: ran out of time or rushed.

This week: red 4, blue 11, black 3.

"Eleven silly mistakes?" her father, Ramesh, asked, peering at the sheet.

"Mostly signs and units," Irawati said. "So next week isn't more chapters. It's checking."

She planned it on a sticky note: every practice set, underline the unit before answering; last five minutes of every mock, check signs only.

The next Saturday: blue 5.

qa.q: How many blue mistakes did Irawati have this week?
How might Irawati have felt when her father asked about the eleven silly mistakes?
qa.a: She seemed calm and focused rather than embarrassed, already knowing what the pattern meant.

qa.q: What else could Irawati do if the red category becomes the biggest?
qa.a: She could plan the next week around revising those concepts with a teacher's help, since red means gaps in understanding.

qa.q: How does the method look to Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh seems surprised at first by the number, but likely reassured to see a clear plan to fix it.

grounding: Shows a student taking a full mock every Saturday, sorting mistakes into concept gaps, careless errors and time pressure, and planning the next week around the biggest.

"What did you get?" Santosh asked, as Rafiq walked out of the Saturday mock hall.

"Doesn't matter yet," Rafiq said. "Tonight's the real work."

"You're weird."

That evening Rafiq sat with his cousin Santosh at the kitchen table, paper spread out. "Every wrong answer goes in one of three boxes. Didn't know it. Knew it but messed up. Ran out of time."

"Okay, question 12."

"Didn't know it. Box one."

They went through all of them. Box one: 9. Box two: 4. Box three: 6.

"So mostly you just don't know stuff," Santosh said.

"Mostly thermodynamics and optics," Rafiq said, circling. "So next week, those two, every evening. And I practise one timed section a day for the time problem."

"And the careless ones?"

"Only four. They can wait."

qa.q: How many answers went in box one?

qa.a: Rafiq seems calm and unbothered by the score, more interested in what the mistakes reveal.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq do after next week's mock?
qa.a: He could compare the three boxes with this week's, to see whether thermodynamics and optics improved.

qa.q: How does the method look to Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh first thinks Rafiq is weird, but by the end is following the logic closely and asking about the careless ones.
